disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive behaviors that are developmentally inappropriate and cause clinically significant impairment in functioning. Symptoms must be present in more than one setting (e.g., work, school, home), have lasted at least six months, and typically begin in childhood, although many individuals are not diagnosed until adulthood when demands exceed coping strategies. The course is often chronic but variable, with periods of partial compensation followed by decompensation under increased cognitive, organizational, or time-management demands. It is differentiated from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by the early onset, pervasiveness across contexts, and primary difficulties with attention regulation, activity level, and impulse control rather than mood state or situational stress alone.

narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Lois was promoted from a more execution-focused sales support role into a client-facing advertising sales strategist position where she suddenly became responsible for juggling multiple complex campaigns, detailed timelines, and frequent presentations. The jump in cognitive load and rapid task-switching strained the informal systems she had always used to keep herself on track, and she began missing internal deadlines, overlooking key details in contracts, and struggling to keep up with the pace of meetings despite long evening hours spent trying to compensate. Her identity as a quiet, reliable professional from a Midwestern background made these lapses especially distressing, and feedback from a new supervisor about her inconsistencies contrasted sharply with her reputation for calm competence. After a formal performance improvement plan was initiated and she found herself re-reading the same planning documents late into the night without feeling any more in control, she sought psychiatric evaluation at the suggestion of an older colleague who had recently been diagnosed with adult ADHD.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I just can’t keep my projects organized anymore, no matter how many lists and calendars I use.

narrative.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Willie transitioned from managing mid-sized construction jobs to leading a series of large, mixed-use developments with tight, overlapping schedules and high financial stakes. The role demanded sustained attention to long coordination meetings, meticulous follow-through on complex task chains, and constant juggling of subcontractors, permitting, and change orders, which exposed longstanding but previously manageable difficulties in staying focused and on track. As projects grew more intricate, he began missing critical details during briefings, reacting impulsively in meetings, and overcompensating with late-night reworking of schedules that still failed to prevent costly oversights, eventually resulting in a near-miss safety incident and formal complaints from both superiors and subcontractors. When an executive review questioned his suitability for the leadership track he’d worked years to attain and he noticed similar patterns affecting his volunteer mentoring commitments and personal relationships, he agreed to see a psychiatrist after a colleague in his trade association described being treated for adult ADHD with similar work struggles.
narrative.chief_complaint: In long meetings and on site, my mind keeps drifting and I can’t seem to stay focused on what people are saying or what I’m supposed to be tracking.

narrative.stressor: Two years ago, Vanisha expanded from being a senior employee at a neighborhood dry cleaner to owning and running her own small boutique operation, taking on responsibility for scheduling, inventory, bookkeeping, and staff oversight in addition to hands-on work. The shift from a structured environment to one she had to organize herself highlighted long-standing but previously masked difficulties in managing multiple streams of information, keeping track of orders, and pacing herself across the day. Despite her disciplined reputation and meticulous receipt-keeping, she found herself increasingly double-booking pickups, misplacing tickets, and jumping between tasks in ways that left her staying late at the shop and bringing paperwork home, which began to strain her energy, church commitments, and time with her spouse. After a mix-up with a wedding gown order led to an irate customer, and her accountant gently questioned why such an organized person was having so many avoidable administrative tangles, she discussed her frustrations with a church friend who suggested an evaluation for possible ADHD and helped her schedule a psychiatric appointment.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep misplacing order tickets and other important things at the shop, and it’s starting to hurt my business.
